slides.0.title: Grape varieties
slides.0.subtitle: The big three, old varieties and Chardonnay Rosé
slides.1.title: The three main grapes and their shares
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Pinot Noir
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Black grape, about 38% of vines, giving structure, body and red fruit
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Chardonnay
slides.1.highlights.1.content: White grape, about 31–32% of vines, giving finesse, citrus and floral notes, high acidity and ageing potential
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Meunier
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Black grape, about 30–31% of vines, giving round fruit and softness, often making NV approachable earlier
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Always state the year
slides.1.highlights.3.content: The Comité Champagne 2025 edition gives 38/32/30; earlier figures were 38/31/31. The gap reflects yearly updates and rounding, so we state the year and do not test the percentages
slides.1.content: Remember "three grapes at about a third each, Pinot Noir slightly ahead", not the decimals.
slides.2.title: What each grape brings to the wine
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Pinot Noir: the frame
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Red fruit (cherry, strawberry), fullness and structure for ageing; most important in the Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Chardonnay: finesse and acidity
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Citrus, white flowers and minerality; reserved when young, developing creamy toasty notes with age; the Côte des Blancs is its heartland
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Meunier: roundness and charm
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Ripens earlier and is more frost-tolerant (later budding), with generous fruit and lower acidity; most typical of the Marne Valley
slides.2.highlights.3.title: The logic of blending
slides.2.highlights.3.content: They complement each other: Chardonnay's acidity and finesse, Pinot Noir's structure, Meunier's fruit and softness; this is the basis of the assemblage
slides.2.content: Black grapes have colourless juice and the colour sits in the skins, so Pinot Noir and Meunier can make white base wine (Blanc de Noirs).
slides.3.title: Old varieties and the 2025 addition of Chardonnay Rosé
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Four "forgotten" varieties
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris are all permitted but together make up under 0.4% of the vineyard (older figures say about 0.3%; sources differ, so not tested)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Chardonnay Rosé
slides.3.highlights.1.content: A pink-berried mutation of Chardonnay recorded in Champagne since about 1900, it dropped out of the specifications through an administrative oversight and was re-authorised in 2025, bringing the permitted varieties to eight
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Dates vary by source
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Some sources give July 2025 for regional approval and others say the EU confirmed it in June 2026. Dates are not tested; just know it was added around 2025 and aims at white base wine, not rosé Champagne
slides.3.highlights.3.title: The disease-resistant Voltis
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Voltis, bred by INRAE and Germany's JKI, is mildew-resistant and was approved for trial at the end of 2022 (up to 5% of a vineyard, up to 10% of a blend). It is a "new variety", separate from the traditional eight, and returns in Level 3
slides.3.content: These minor varieties symbolise options under climate change, yet remain very rare on labels and in the market.
slides.4.title: Linking grapes to styles and sub-regions
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Blanc de Blancs
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Made only from white grapes (in practice almost always Chardonnay), fine and bright, typified by the Côte des Blancs
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Blanc de Noirs
slides.4.highlights.1.content: White wine from black grapes only (Pinot Noir and/or Meunier), fuller and more red-fruited
slides.4.highlights.2.title: The dominant grape per sub-region
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Montagne de Reims and Côte des Bar: Pinot Noir; Marne Valley: Meunier; Côte des Blancs: Chardonnay. It is the first step in predicting style
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Where this connects
slides.4.highlights.3.content: For Burgundy's Pinot Noir and Chardonnay and the Chablis comparison, see the Burgundy course; for Crémant and Cava grape differences, see the Level 3 comparison lesson
slides.4.content: Sub-region × grape × winemaking are the three dials for predicting Champagne style.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What does Blanc de Noirs mean?
A. Made only from white grapes
C. Rosé made by skin contact
D. White wine made from black grapes (Pinot Noir and/or Meunier)
Black grapes have colourless juice, so gentle pressing gives white base wine.
Which best describes Meunier's role in a blend?
A. The highest acidity and minerality
B. Round fruit and softness, often making the wine approachable earlier
Chardonnay supplies acidity and finesse, Pinot Noir structure, Meunier fruit and softness.
Which group consists entirely of permitted Champagne varieties?
A. Pinot Noir, Chenin Blanc, Meunier
C. Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc
Each other group contains a non-permitted variety (Chenin Blanc, Riesling, Gamay).
